I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm that it is of an acceptable scientific standard, however I have significant reservations, as outlined above.

This article is focused on a database made with records reporting the concentration of CO2 and other environmental parameters measured in two hostels belonging to a university campus. The text of the article is clear and understandable, the document is well structured, but it has poor originality and its novelty is not clear or ambiguous; moreover, it is featured by serious flaws.

The introduction does not offer an adequate background to the topic. There is a huge scientific literature reporting the issues related to the use of Iot devices for environmental monitoring completely ignored by authors. A lot of similar works related to the issue addressed by this paper are currently present in the scientific panorama, but the authors did not perform an adequate comparison between their work with the similar ones as they should do.

The study design and the methods are poorly described, so that it is almost impossible to replicate the experiment. In particular, the authors did not provide information about how many sensors were used in the experiment and where they were placed, moreover no information about the characteristics of the monitored places were reported. It is not known the volume of the monitored spaces, and also how many occupants were there over the duration of the experiment. These elements have a huge influence on the monitored variables, but no information were reported. Another aspect to consider is that almost no information is available about the device built by the authors and the electronic components composing it. There is just a picture showing an electric scheme, but the electronic component pins are not reported in the scheme, so it is impossible to replicate it. It is also not clear why the authors used a home-made device to perform the measurements while there are a lot of devices available on the market to do it.

The results are poorly presented and commented. The text in the pictures are totally unreadable and no analysis was carried out on the dataset produced; moreover, comparisons with similar datasets or measurements performed in previous works are not present. The reliability and accuracy of the measures are questionable, unconvincing or ambiguous, as matter of facts, it is the first time that a CO2 mean concentration of 0 ppm is measured in an indoor monitored space.

As the methods and the results are unconvincing, the conclusion cannot rely on solid basis.

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to state that I do not consider it to be of an acceptable scientific standard, for reasons outlined above.

The article presents an environmental dataset collected via IoT sensors (SCD30 and digital light sensors) deployed in male and female hostels at Bowen University, Nigeria. The dataset records four key variables: temperature, humidity, carbon dioxide (CO₂) concentration, and light intensity. Data were collected over 14 days and analyzed using summary statistics and scatter matrix plots to understand variable distributions and interdependencies. The resulting dataset is publicly available via Mendeley.

                    Writing quality is inconsistent: some sections (like scatter plot interpretations) are redundant or overgeneralized. Suggestions for improvement: 
                Clarify which specific studies your work complements or expands upon.
                    Tighten descriptions of figures and plots; interpret key findings beyond mere correlation.
                    Improve sentence structure and clarity throughout the Results and Discussion sections.

Summary of Manuscript:This systematic review and meta-analysis assessed clinical outcomes in tuberculosis patients with drug-induced liver injury (TB-DILI). Analyzing data from five studies involving 5,798 patients, it found that TB-DILI did not significantly affect 2-month sputum conversion. However, patients without DILI had significantly higher treatment success rates and lower mortality risk.

Overall Assessment: Overall, the authors have provided a comprehensive review on the impact of DILI on TB treatment management. The outcomes assessed are also highly applicable, as they include conversion rates and mortality. However, several inconsistencies in the methods and results limit the validity of the study's findings.

General Comment:

I appreciate the opportunity to review this article, titled 
                “Assessment of the Level of Knowledge, Attitude, and Preference for Myopia Management Among Patients and University Students in Trinidad.".This manuscript addresses a highly relevant and timely topic, not only for Trinidad but also as a public health issue of global significance in eye care. The study is well-conducted and demonstrates potential to contribute meaningfully to the existing body of knowledge. However, I believe that with some revisions to the manuscript, it can achieve the level of rigor required for acceptance. Below, I have outlined specific comments and suggestions that, if addressed, could substantially enhance the overall quality and impact of the article.

Article summary:

The paper sought to understand the knowledge, attitudes, and preferences regarding myopia management within a sample of 317 participants aged 18–40. It highlighted significant gaps in knowledge about myopia and identified spectacles and contact lenses as the most preferred corrective measures. While the study further found that attitudes toward myopia management were generally positive, it emphasized the need for targeted educational interventions to enhance awareness and improve management strategies in Trinidad.

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm that it is of an acceptable scientific standard, however I have significant reservations, as outlined above.

This is an overall engaging and clinically relevant study. The authors investigate a novel hypothesis—whether serum biomarker concentrations vary by sampling location and following a brief non-weight-bearing exercise intervention. The use of local venous sampling from the saphenous vein is innovative, and the short-duration exercise protocol enhances feasibility in diverse clinical settings.

However, several methodological and interpretive aspects require further clarification or revision:

Sampling Site Justification

While local venous sampling is promising, the choice of the saphenous vein warrants further discussion. As noted by another reviewer, the popliteal vein may be a more direct proxy for joint efflux. Moreover, although less practical on a larger scale, synovial fluid remains the most joint-specific matrix and should be more critically discussed as a comparator.

Lack of Post-Exercise Knee Sampling

The omission of knee samples post-exercise is a missed opportunity. Assessing local changes after intervention would directly test whether this site is more sensitive to mechanical or metabolic changes than systemic sites. A rationale for its exclusion is needed.

Group Comparability and Bias

The study suffers from notable group imbalances, particularly between the control and KOA groups (e.g., age, BMI). Additionally, the mixed ethnic composition of participants could influence biomarker levels. Prior research (Refer to 1) shows ethnicity can significantly affect inflammatory markers. These confounders should be acknowledged or controlled for analytically.

Disease Characterization

It would strengthen the manuscript to report disease status with greater granularity (e.g., Kellgren & Lawrence grading, MRI features). This would allow correction for disease severity and improve interpretation of biomarker variability.

Statistical Approach

While the authors use standard statistical methods appropriately for a pilot study, more advanced techniques are better suited for the data structure:

Linear or Generalized Linear Mixed Models (LMM/GLMM) would account for repeated measures, missing data, and inter-individual variation.

MANOVA could assess interaction effects across multiple, correlated biomarkers.

Adjustment for multiple comparisons (e.g., FDR correction) is essential to mitigate the risk of false positives given the exploratory nature and small sample size.

Biomarker Interpretation and Methodological Details

The finding of reduced IL-1β in KOA is intriguing but underexplained. Given its known pro-inflammatory role, further mechanistic or assay-specific interpretation is warranted.

Reliance on subjective exercise intensity (Borg RPE) may introduce variability; objective metrics (e.g., heart rate or ergometer wattage) should be considered in future protocols.

Figure legends lack sufficient explanatory detail and would benefit from improved interpretive commentary.

Specific Recommendations:

Apply linear mixed-effects modeling to better handle repeated measures and missing data.

Consider multivariate or dimensionality reduction approaches (e.g., PCA) to explore biomarker profiles holistically.

Adjust for covariates such as age, BMI, and ethnicity in comparative analyses.

Correct for multiple testing to improve statistical reliability.

Expand discussion on IL-6 and leptin’s location-based variation, considering local adipose contributions and vascular differences.

Clarify whether IL-6 elevations post-exercise reflect inflammatory signaling or mechanical/metabolic responses.

Authors: Oliver O'Sullivan, Miranda Merwyn Raj,  Abdullah Alshammari, Alexander N. Bennett, Richard Pearson, Stefan Kluzek.

This case-control pilot study aims to understand the effect of two ‘experimental variables’, the location of sampling and a short, non-weight-bearing, sub-maximal exercise intervention. A few typical serum biomarkers in OA. The key hypothesis of this study is: serum concentration of biomarkers will be higher nearer to the joint than those measured in the systemic circulation.

I have following observations on this study:

Comment 1.

The authors propose that sampling blood closer to the joint may offer a more accurate representation of the joint environment by minimizing dilution in the systemic circulation, to my opinion, this hypothesis holds merit. However, I have serious reservations regarding their choice of the saphenous vein for sampling. Anatomically, the saphenous vein primarily drains blood from superficial tissues such as the skin and subcutaneous fat of the medial leg and thigh, rather than from deeper joint structures, not certainly the knee. Consequently, it is unlikely to carry joint-specific biomarkers. In my view, the popliteal vein accessible through the popliteal fossa would be a more appropriate choice, as it directly drains blood from the knee joint and is therefore more likely to reflect joint-specific pathological changes. Selection of saphenous vein defeats the very purpose of their hypothesis.

Comment 2:

I also have concerns regarding the control group selected by the authors. In addition to the small sample size, there is a significant gender imbalance—three females in the control group and none in the KOA group. Furthermore, the ethnic composition is inconsistent, with seven Indian participants in the control group and only one in the KOA group. Age matching is also inadequate, as the median age in the control group is 26.5, while it is 52.0 in the KOA group. The authors should recognize that such discrepancies in the control group compromise the reliability of the data and may lead to inconclusive or misleading results.

Comment 3:

Considering this as a pilot study, and in an effort to encourage the authors, I am voting in favour of the indexing of this manuscript after addressing/justifying the above comments. I do so with the expectation that the authors will incorporate the critical suggestions provided into the more comprehensive version of their study.
